caption: Are We Fast Yet's Mandelbrot, 140 laps, the same source on both, run at once: Pharo 12 (Cog) on the left, Samaltak on the right. Each line: one lap, in ms of CPU time. On screen the race runs at about {speed}× real speed.
spoken: Same benchmark, same source code: Pharo 12 on the left, Samaltak on the right. Each line is one lap, in milliseconds.

caption: Samaltak is done: first lap, steady state (median of the second half) and total, in CPU time. Pharo is still running.
spoken: Samaltak's done. Pharo takes about three times as long.

caption: src/VM-Jit, 15,090 lines in 23 files: the baseline compiler, the optimizing one (Opt…), the runtime and assembler they share. Translated to C in vm/gen.
spoken: The jit's written in Smalltalk: a baseline compiler and an optimizing one, about fifteen thousand lines, translated to C like the rest of the VM.

caption: JitRuntime>>defaults: baseline code after 2 activations, optimized code after 1000 activations and backward jumps.
spoken: Every method starts out interpreted. Its third call compiles it with baseline, and after a thousand calls or loop iterations, opt compiles it again.

caption: Complex>>- has no machine code yet (jitSendSites is nil). Ten calls later it has baseline code, and each inline cache that was used holds the class it saw.
spoken: This one has no machine code yet. Ten calls later it does, and its inline caches have recorded what they saw: Complex.

caption: Complex>>+ as baseline compiled it: the inline cache's class check at the entry, a call through each send's cache, inline SmallInteger arithmetic.
spoken: Here's baseline code for adding two complex numbers. An inline cache check on the receiver's class, a call through its own cache for each send, and inline arithmetic, with tag checks and an overflow branch.
cues: a call through its own cache

caption: The same method from opt, compiled from that feedback: class guards, inlined activations, Floats added in d registers, a deoptimization stub per guard.
spoken: Opt compiles it again from what those caches saw. Now the sends are inlined: the accessors behind a class guard, the floats added in FP registers, and a failed guard deoptimizes.
cues: the floats added in FP registers

caption: MandelbrotView>>pixelFor:, inlined into the render loop: the inside of the set from black to red, ⌘S while it renders.
spoken: Opt inlined pixelFor: into the render loop. I'll make the inside of the set red, and save while it's rendering.

caption: The optimized code that inlined it is invalidated; the render carries on with the new method: red from that row down. The counters just before and after ⌘S.
spoken: The code that inlined it gets thrown out, the loop just carries on, and the red shows from that row down.

caption: Measured here, on the work clock (CPU work at a nominal 3.3 GHz): Mandelbrot in this system on baseline only, then on opt again (Smalltalk vm jitParameters:), the median of 7 runs each.
spoken: Here's that benchmark in this system, switched to baseline only, and now back to opt.

caption: Pharo 12's VM (libPharoVMCore.dylib): CoInterpreter and StackToRegisterMappingCogit, VMMaker's production Cogit: one machine-code method per method, sends through inline caches.
spoken: Pharo 12's VM runs Cog's StackToRegisterMappingCogit: like our baseline, it compiles one method at a time, and never inlines.

caption: docs/jit.md: Are We Fast Yet (14 benchmarks, headless, steady state): baseline 0.64 and opt 0.33 of Pharo 12's time, both faster on all 14. Compiling: baseline as fast as Cog; opt about 7× baseline per bytecode, inlined bytecode included.
spoken: In headless runs of Are We Fast Yet, baseline takes sixty-four percent of Pharo's time, and opt thirty-three.

caption: docs/benchmarks.md, real-world workloads: 16 programs written against each system's own library: opt 0.32 and baseline 0.41 of Pharo 14's time, both faster on all 16.
spoken: On sixteen real-world programs using each system's own library, opt takes thirty-two percent of Pharo's time, baseline forty-one, and both win all sixteen.

caption: Two compilers, written in Smalltalk, live in one running image, driven through samaltak-ctl.
spoken: Two compilers, both Smalltalk, in one running image.
